newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark ends European trade just shy of 3-wk lows.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark ends European trade just shy of 3-wk lows.

text.p: The dollar skidded to fresh three-week troughs against the mark in late Europe, snubbing robust growth in U.S. housing starts, as key support levels failed to stem the German unit's momentum.
"The dollar is not looking good. It looks like it could go lower on mark strength across-the-board," said a trader at a Danish bank.
The dollar slumped to end the European session down 1.3 pfennings at 1.6771/74 marks from 1.6897/04 marks in late Europe on Monday, though just off lows at 1.6750 marks.
The U.S. unit stumbled as key support levels failed.
Chartists had said a push below support at 1.6840/60 marks would render dollar/mark shaky.

"Dollar/mark is still under pressure and 1.6840/60 is critical here to avoid the 1.6680-zone and the prospect of establishing a medium-term top," said Gerry Celaya, senior technical analyst at American Express Bank in London.

The German unit, mostly firmer after a fresh bout of European Monetary Union (EMU) uncertainty, was just off its perch in late dealings after its earlier sprint to four-month peaks against the lira and one-year highs against the Swedish crown.

The German unit's renewed bout of strength on Tuesday followed comments by Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, who in unusually strong words for a member of the German central bank, said a delay to EMU was the only option if Germany does not strictly fulfil the Maastricht Treaty.

In an interview with "Boerse Online" magazine, Kuehbacher said he saw little chance that Bonn would be able to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product as is mandated for nations hoping to join monetary union and that failure to do so meant delaying EMU.
That, said traders, gave a fresh lift to the mark.
Analysts and traders, however, have also said the mark's strength this week has been fuelled by expectations for positive German data this week.
Key German data this week, including the IFO survey and M3 supply, could mitigate perceptions for higher rates in the U.S. after robust data, including housing starts released on Tuesday.
Total U.S. housing starts shot up 12.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.53 million in February - the strongest pace since March 1994.
"The housing numbers were quite strong," said David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel.
U.S. interest rates are back in the spotlight as the market awaits next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, which could, said some analysts set higher rates.
"The market has factored in a good possibility of a Fed rate hike," said Bloom.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to the Joint Economic Committee on Thursday will also be watched closely for clues on U.S. monetary policy.
"Greenspan has seemed to indicate that he would prefer some pre-emptive tightening, it's a very close call but the market risk is that he won't raise rates," said a German bank dealer.
Against the yen, the dollar was also softer in late Europe and stood at 122.45 yen vs 123.55/65 late Monday.
Japanese government plans announced overnight to improve land liquidity to help solve the problem of financial firms' problem loans pressured dollar/yen in early trade
-- Julia Meehan, London newsroom +4471 542 6701
